{{Short description|Self-similar curve related to golden ratio}}
[[File:GoldenSpiralLogarithmic_color_in.gif|thumb|Golden spirals are [[self-similar]]. The shape is infinitely repeated when magnified.]]

In [[geometry]], a '''golden spiral''' is a [[logarithmic spiral]] whose growth factor is {{math|&phi;}}, the [[golden ratio]].<ref>Chang, Yu-sung, "[http://demonstrations.wolfram.com/GoldenSpiral/ Golden Spiral] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190728084311/http://demonstrations.wolfram.com/GoldenSpiral/ |date=2019-07-28 }}", [[The Wolfram Demonstrations Project]].</ref> That is, a golden spiral gets wider (or further from its origin) by a factor of {{math|&phi;}} for every quarter [[Turn (angle)|turn]] it makes.

== Approximations of the golden spiral ==
[[File:FakeRealLogSpiral.svg|right|thumb|Approximate and true golden spirals: the <span style= color:black;background-color:lime>green</span> spiral is made from quarter-circles [[tangency|tangent]] to the interior of each square, while the <span style= color:white;background-color:red>red</span> spiral is a golden spiral, a special type of [[logarithmic spiral]]. Overlapping portions appear <span style="background-color:yellow;color: black">yellow</span>. The length of the side of a larger square to the next smaller square is in the [[golden ratio]]. For a square with side length 1, the next smaller square is {{nowrap|1/φ}} wide. The next width is {{nowrap|1/φ²}}, then {{nowrap|1/φ³}}, and so on.]]

There are several comparable spirals that approximate, but do not exactly equal, a golden spiral.<ref name=madden>{{cite book|last=Madden|first=Charles B.|title=Fib and Phi in Music: The Golden Proportion Musical Form|isbn=978-0967172767|publisher=High Art Press|year=2005|orig-year=1999|pages=14–16|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JhnERQLm4lUC}}</ref>

For example, a golden spiral can be approximated by first starting with a [[rectangle]] for which the ratio between its length and width is the golden ratio. This rectangle can then be partitioned into a [[square]] and a [[similarity (geometry)|similar]] rectangle and this rectangle can then be split in the same way. After continuing this process for an arbitrary number of steps, the result will be an almost complete partitioning of the rectangle into squares. The corners of these squares can be connected by quarter-[[circle]]s. The result, though not a true [[logarithmic spiral]], closely approximates a golden spiral.<ref name=madden/>

Another approximation is a [[Fibonacci number|Fibonacci spiral]], which is constructed slightly differently. A Fibonacci spiral starts with a rectangle partitioned into 2 squares. In each step, a square the length of the rectangle's longest side is added to the rectangle. Since the ratio between consecutive [[Fibonacci number]]s approaches the [[golden ratio]] as the Fibonacci numbers approach infinity, so too does this spiral get more similar to the previous approximation the more squares are added, as illustrated by the image.

A study explored the aesthetic preference between different spirals, focusing on the golden spiral and the Fibonacci spiral. In an online experiment comprising 106 participants, the golden spiral was found to be significantly preferred over the Fibonacci spiral (79.2% vs. 20.8%), primarily due to the continuity of its [[curvature]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Golden spiral or Fibonacci spiral: Which is more beautiful and why?|last=Hübner|first=Ronald|journal=i-Perception|issue=2|doi=10.1177/20416695241243319|year=2024|volume=15|article-number=20416695241243319 |doi-access=free|pmid=38600988 |pmc=11005508}}</ref>

==Spirals in nature==
It is sometimes erroneously stated that spiral galaxies and [[nautilus]] shells get wider in the pattern of a golden spiral, and hence are related to both {{math|&phi;}} and the Fibonacci series.<ref>
For example, these books:

 }}, 
{{cite book

 | publisher = HarperCollins
 | year = 2011
 | isbn = 978-0062024473
 | page = 162
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=TosVluTfLOEC&pg=PA162
 }}, 
{{cite book

 | author = Charles Seife
 | publisher = Penguin
 | year = 2000
 | isbn = 978-0140296471

 }}, 
{{cite book

 | publisher = Llewellyn Worldwide
 | year = 2008
 | isbn = 9780738713533

In truth, many [[mollusk]] shells including nautilus shells exhibit logarithmic spiral growth, but at a variety of [[angle]]s usually distinctly different from that of the golden spiral.<ref>
{{cite book
 | title = The Universal Book of Mathematics: From Abracadabra to Zeno's Paradoxes
 | author = David Darling
 | publisher = John Wiley & Sons
 | year = 2004
 | isbn = 9780471270478
 | page = 188
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=nnpChqstvg0C&pg=PA188
 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Devlin|first=Keith|title=The myth that will not go away|url=http://www.maa.org/external_archive/devlin/devlin_05_07.html|date=May 2007|access-date=2013-12-09|archive-date=2020-11-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112034625/https://www.maa.org/external_archive/devlin/devlin_05_07.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Peterson|first=Ivars|title=Sea Shell Spirals|url=http://www.sciencenews.org/view/generic/id/6030/title/Sea_Shell_Spirals|work=Science News|publisher=Society for Science & the Public|date=2005-04-01|access-date=2011-10-08|archive-date=2012-10-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121003045834/http://www.sciencenews.org/view/generic/id/6030/title/Sea_Shell_Spirals|url-status=dead}}</ref> Although spiral galaxies have often been modeled as logarithmic spirals, [[Archimedean spiral]]s, or [[hyperbolic spiral]]s, their pitch angles vary with distance from the galactic center, unlike logarithmic spirals (for which this angle does not vary), and also at variance with the other mathematical spirals used to model them.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Savchenko | first1 = S. S.
 | last2 = Reshetnikov | first2 = V. P.
 | date = September 2013
 | doi = 10.1093/mnras/stt1627
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
 | pages = 1074–1083
 | title = Pitch angle variations in spiral galaxies
 | volume = 436| doi-access = free
 | arxiv = 1309.4308
 }}</ref>
[[Phyllotaxis]], the pattern of plant growth, is in some case connected with the golden ratio  because it involves successive leaves or petals being separated by the [[golden angle]]. Although this can sometimes be associated with spiral forms, such as in [[sunflower]] seed heads,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ridley|first=J.N.|date=February 1982|title=Packing efficiency in sunflower heads|journal=Mathematical Biosciences|language=en|volume=58|issue=1|pages=129–139|doi=10.1016/0025-5564(82)90056-6}}</ref> these are more closely related to [[Fermat spiral]]s than logarithmic spirals.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Vogel | first = Helmut
 | date = June 1979
 | doi = 10.1016/0025-5564(79)90080-4
 | issue = 3–4
 | journal = Mathematical Biosciences
 | pages = 179–189
 | title = A better way to construct the sunflower head
 | volume = 44}}</ref>

==Mathematics==
[[File:Fibonacci Spiral.svg|thumb|A Fibonacci spiral approximates the golden spiral using quarter-circle arcs inscribed in squares derived from the [[Fibonacci number|Fibonacci sequence]].]]
A golden spiral with initial radius 1 is the locus of points of [[polar coordinates]] <math>(r,\theta)</math> satisfying
<math display=block>r = \varphi^{2\theta/\pi},</math>
where <math>\varphi</math> is the golden ratio. This means that r is multiplied by a factor of <math>\varphi</math> every 90 degrees turned.

The [[polar equation]] for a golden spiral is the same as for other [[logarithmic spiral]]s, but with a special value of the growth factor {{mvar|b}}:<ref>{{cite book | title = Divine Proportion: {{math|&Phi;}} Phi in Art, Nature, and Science | author = Priya Hemenway | isbn = 1-4027-3522-7 | publisher = Sterling Publishing Co | year = 2005 | pages = 127–129}}</ref>
<math display="block">r = ae^{b\theta}</math>
or
<math display=block>\theta = \frac{1}{b} \ln(r/a),</math>
with {{mvar|[[e (mathematical constant)|e]]}} being the base of [[natural logarithm]]s, {{mvar|a}} being the initial radius of the spiral, and {{mvar|b}} such that when {{mvar|&theta;}} is a [[right angle]] (a quarter turn in either direction):
<math display=block>e^{b\theta_\mathrm{right}} = \varphi.</math>

Therefore, {{mvar|b}} is given by
<math display=block>b = {\ln{\varphi} \over \theta_\mathrm{right}}.</math>

[[File:Lucas number spiral.svg|200x120px|thumb|right|The [[Lucas number|Lucas]] spiral approximates the golden spiral when its terms are large but not when they are small. 10 terms, from 2 to 76, are included.]]
The numerical value of {{mvar|b}} depends on whether the right angle is measured as 90 [[degree (angle)|degrees]] or as <math>\textstyle\frac{\pi}{2}</math> [[radian]]s; and since the angle can be in either direction, it is easiest to write the formula for the absolute value of {{mvar|b}} (that is, {{mvar|b}} can also be the negative of this value):
<math display=block>|b| = {\ln{\varphi} \over 90} \doteq 0.0053468</math>
for {{mvar|&theta;}} in degrees, or
<math display=block>|b| = {\ln{\varphi} \over \pi/2} \doteq 0.3063489</math>
for {{mvar|&theta;}} in radians.<ref>{{cite OEIS|A212225}}</ref>

An alternate formula for a logarithmic and golden spiral is<ref>{{cite book | title = Symmetries of Nature: A Handbook for Philosophy of Nature and Science | author = Klaus Mainzer | pages = 45, 199–200 | year = 1996 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=rqzaQo6CaA0C&dq=%22golden+spiral%22+log&pg=PA200| isbn = 3-11-012990-6 | publisher = Walter de Gruyter }}</ref>
<math display=block>r = ac^{\theta}</math>
where the constant {{mvar|c}} is given by
<math display=block>c = e^b</math>
which for the golden spiral gives {{mvar|c}} values of
<math display=block>c = \varphi ^ \frac{1}{90} \doteq 1.0053611</math>
if {{mvar|&theta;}} is measured in degrees, and
<math display=block>c = \varphi ^ \frac{2}{\pi} \doteq 1.358456</math>
if {{mvar|&theta;}} is measured in radians.<ref>{{cite OEIS|A212224}}</ref>

With respect to logarithmic spirals the golden spiral has the distinguishing property
that for four [[collinear]] spiral points ''A'', ''B'', ''C'', ''D'' belonging to arguments   
{{math|&theta;}}, {{math|&theta; + &pi;}}, {{math|&theta; + 2&pi;}}, {{math|&theta; + 3&pi;}}
the point ''C'' is the [[projective harmonic conjugate]] of ''B'' with respect to ''A'', ''D'', i.e. the [[cross ratio]] (''A'',''D'';''B'',''C'') has the singular value −1. 
The golden spiral is the only logarithmic spiral with (''A'',''D'';''B'',''C'') = (''A'',''D'';''C'',''B'').

===Polar slope===
[[File:Spiral-log-st-se.svg|thumb|upright=0.8|Definition of slope angle and sector]]

In the polar equation for a [[logarithmic spiral]]:
<math display=block>r = ae^{b\theta}</math>
the parameter {{mvar|b}} is related to the polar slope angle <math>\alpha</math>:
<math display=block>\tan\alpha=b. </math>

In a golden spiral, <math>b</math> being constant and equal to <math>|b| = {\ln{\varphi} \over \pi/2} </math> (for {{mvar|&theta;}} in radians, as defined above), the slope angle <math>\alpha</math> is
<math display=block>\alpha = \arctan(|b|) = \arctan\left({\ln{\varphi} \over \pi/2}\right),</math>
hence
<math display=block>\alpha \doteq 17.03239113</math>
if measured in degrees, or
<math display=block>\alpha \doteq 0.2972713047</math>
if measured in radians.<ref>{{cite OEIS|A335605}}</ref>

Its [[complementary angle]]
<math display=block>\beta = \pi/2 - \alpha \doteq 1.273525022</math>
in radians, or
<math display=block>\beta = 90 - \alpha \doteq 73</math>
in degrees, is the angle the golden spiral arms make with a line from the center of the spiral.
